Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:20: Also in the Tikkunim (page 59b) - see there - they explained several particulars concerning the matter of theft. And from there we learn that the matter of repentance applies to the commandments, and even to precision in the commandments - such as whether one occupied himself with Torah properly or not. And along these lines the reader may infer, for all matters where some blemish is fitting, that repentance is required, and he is called a "ba'al teshuvah" - for since the supernal levels are damaged by his sin, and he is one who restores the water to its place, it is fitting that he be called "ba'al teshuvah."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:21: They said there, of blessed memory: further, the commandment [against] "the spoil of the poor is in your houses" (Isaiah 3:14) - this is the Shechinah, for whoever robs the prayer, which is charity to the Righteous One, the Life of the worlds, comprising eighteen blessings, it is as though he robbed him of his life, which is the Shechinah, of whom it is said (Ecclesiastes 9:9), "enjoy life with the wife whom you love." And so whoever diminishes from the delight of Shabbat, it is as though he robbed his Shechinah, who is Shabbat, the unique daughter - and this caused her to be robbed from him in exile, this is what is written (Isaiah 50:1), "and for your transgressions your mother was sent away." And what is repentance? (Leviticus 5:23), "then he shall restore the theft which he has stolen" - that he restore the Shechinah to her place. "Or the thing taken by extortion which he took by extortion" - this is the Holy One, blessed be He, from whom she is separated - for the Shechinah is called the positive commandments from the side of the right, and the negative commandments from the side of the left, and Torah is called from the side of the middle pillar - and whoever robs or extorts in Torah and in the positive and negative commandments, it is as though he robbed the Shechinah from the arms of the Holy One, blessed be He. And so from the side of Yesod, the Life of the worlds, are called the commandment[s] - the commandment of circumcision - whoever robs in the covenant and brings forth his seed to a foreign domain, it is as though he brought it out from a private domain to a public domain, and caused the Shechinah to go out from her place, which is the Land of Israel, which is a private domain, and exiled her among the nations of the world, who are a public domain - this is what is written, "and for your transgressions your mother was sent away." And therefore (Exodus 20:7), "you shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain" - what is "the name of your God"? This is the Shechinah; "in vain" - this is idolatry, to which she was exiled - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:22: Behold, it is proven from the discourse that one who is obligated in a matter and does not do it is called a robber, as he said, "robs in Torah and in the positive commandments" - and this is along the lines of withholding a hired worker's wages, which is akin to robbery.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:23: And so they also explained in Midrash Rabbah, in Parashat Bamidbar, in these words: another interpretation, "do not cut off," and so on (Numbers 4:18) - this is what is written (Proverbs 22:22), "do not rob the poor, because he is poor." Our Rabbis said, of what does the verse speak? If he is poor, what does he have to rob? Rather, it speaks only of the gifts owed to the poor, which one is obligated to give them by the Torah - gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field, and the tithe for the poor - and the Holy One, blessed be He, warned that a person not rob from them the gifts fitting to give them, "because he is poor" - his poverty is enough for him; it is not enough that the rich man stands at ease while the poor man is in distress, but he even robs from him what the Holy One, blessed be He, gave him - to this point. And along these lines this applies to the matter of robbing Torah and commandments, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:24: And behold, through this explanation of the verse that Rashbi, peace be upon him, gave concerning "he shall restore the theft," we know from this the nature of repentance, both for positive and negative commandments - for they said that one who is negligent, whether in a positive commandment, a negative commandment, or occupation with Torah, it is all as though he robbed the Shechinah from the arms of the Holy One, blessed be He. If so, repentance is always to restore the Shechinah to the Holy One, blessed be He, between both arms - meaning, with fear and with love, as will be further explained, that this is His repentance, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:25: However, the punishments vary according to the nature of the transgressions, between positive and negative commandments, as will be explained concerning the four categories of atonement - just as the matter of theft is not equal, for one steals a penny and another steals a hundred coins - so too it is not equal for one who steals the king's wife from between the king's arms and uncovers her outside his house, outside his palace, versus one who uncovers her among the nations of the world - and this is the matter of repentance according to weight, for one must weigh how great the blemish was, and suffer accordingly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:26: And one must further know, concerning the matter of repentance, that in all the places we explained in the Gate of Fear where iniquity blemishes, in all of them repentance is required.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:27: We explained in general that the blemish reaches Atzilut, and reaches the inner throne through Israel's iniquities, blemishes the angels, blemishes the world - for the world is called "half meritorious, half liable," and it tips the whole world to the scale of liability - it blemishes the body of the Torah, for marks are made in it, and all the holy ones and the Shechinah depart from it, and likewise his holy soul departs from him, especially concerning anger, as explained in Parashat Tetzaveh (page 182b) - and when the soul departs, the Shechinah also departs, for the soul is a part of her, as explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 62, page 94b), in these words: and concerning that soul given to a person, it is said (Genesis 1:27), "and God created man in His image" - in the image of the Shechinah. And he further says on: whoever blemishes this image, it is as though he diminishes the likeness, and the Shechinah does not rest there - and the secret of the matter (Deuteronomy 31:17), "because our God is not among us, have these evils found us?" - the evils found me once the Shechinah departed from me - to this point. Behold, it is explicit that when a person blemishes the image of his soul, he literally blemishes the Shechinah, from whom the image of the soul's likeness was created, and the soul and the Shechinah, both together, depart from him, and then the external forces rule over him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:28: And Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in Parashat Naso (Zohar, page 123a), that when the spirit of impurity rests upon a person, he is then called "dead" - and this is [why] "the wicked, in their lifetime, are called dead" - and he says there that the Shechinah, who is the final heh, is the breath through which a person is sustained, along the lines of "for by everything that proceeds from the mouth of the LORD does man live" (Deuteronomy 8:3), as we copied in the Gate of Love, chapter 10 - and he says, this heh does not depart from the body, and through her it exists; and when she departs from him, behold, the deadly poison comes and rests upon him, called impurity, idolatry, disqualification, the Angel of Death, darkness and gloom, and it rests upon a person's body, and at that time the person is called dead - and the secret of the matter (Ezekiel 18:32), "for I have no pleasure in the death of him who dies, says the Lord GOD; wherefore turn yourselves, and live."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:29: And they said further on, that just as there is an image of holiness, which is the Shechinah, from which flows holiness to a person, that he fulfill the 248 commandments that are her image, so there is an external image resting upon him to cause him to sin - and when a person sins, that evil image rests upon him, and according to his sin, so does it clothe him. And therefore, when he returns [in repentance] at first, he must strip from himself this spirit of impurity and abandon it forever - and it is good for him to enter the mikveh to strip this impurity from himself, and so they wrote in Sefer Chassidim. And we may infer this from the matter of the immersion of a convert - for in order for him to enter into holiness, if he does not immerse he has done nothing; so it is with the wicked man who goes forth - in order to enter into holiness, after he accepts upon himself not to return to his iniquity, he shall immerse, and not be one who immerses while still holding a creeping thing [i.e., the sin] in his hand.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:30: And by holding fast to repentance and its conditions, which we shall explain, with God's help, he repairs all the levels he has blemished - and so they said (Zohar, Parashat Naso, page 122b): Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Yehuda were walking from Usha to Lod. Rabbi Yehuda said, let us say words of Torah - "if a man opens a pit, or if a man digs a pit," and so on (Exodus 21:33) - what is written after it? "The owner of the pit shall pay." And if this is so [for a mere pit], how much more so one who causes the world evil through his sins! But I am astonished: even though one has caused the world evil, why does he have repentance, when it is written (Numbers 5:6), "a man or woman, when they commit any sin of man," and so on, "then they shall confess their sin which they have done, and he shall restore"? Rather, certainly this avails them, because he does repentance - as it were, he actually repairs it himself, for what he blemished above, he repairs it. And through what? Through repentance - and repentance repairs everything: it repairs above, it repairs below, it repairs himself, it repairs the whole world - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:31: And behold, according to Rabbi Yehuda's view, this "Teshuvah" is the supernal Mother, as is proven further on from Rabbi Yitzchak's words - and this repentance "repairs above" - the blemish in Atzilut; "repairs below" - the worlds from the Shechinah downward, the throne and the angels; "repairs himself" - the blemish within him, that departed, like the story told in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, page 75b), and likewise the soul that departed from him, and likewise the Shechinah that returns to him, as he says (Malachi 3:7), "return to Me, and I will return to you," and King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 51:14), "restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and let a willing spirit uphold me."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:32: And according to Rabbi Yitzchak's words, the repentance every person performs is below - for not every person has the power to perform such an excellent repentance that it ascends all the way above, as in the case of King David's repentance, peace be upon him. In these words: come and see, even the Community of Israel is called "teshuvah" - and should you say that the supernal repentance is not found everywhere - rather, this is called "teshuvah" when mercy returns to receive her, and she returns over all the hosts and nurses them; and it is the complete repentance when the soul is given over to her, and she takes it, at the time she is in [the state of] repentance - then everything is repaired above and below, and he is repaired, and the whole world is repaired - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:33: And behold, through these discourses mentioned, we shall understand what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Yoma (86a): great is repentance, for it reaches up to the Throne of Glory, as it is said (Hosea 14:2), "return, O Israel, to the LORD your God." And the intent is that a person, according to the level of his soul, so does he blemish at the [corresponding] levels - for if he has only a nefesh, all his blemishing is in the modes that are in Asiyah, where the Shechinah dwells in this world; and if he has a ru'ach, he blemishes higher up; and with a neshamah, he blemishes the throne, from which the souls are hewn, as explained above in the Tikkunim. And one who has a soul of Atzilut does not come to sin at all, as we copied in the Gate of Fear. And this is the virtue of repentance, that it repairs even if the blemish rose so high that it reached the throne.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:34: And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in the Midrash (Yalkut Hosea, section 532): Rabbi Yuda bar Rabbi Simon [said], "return, O Israel, to the LORD your God" - even if you have denied the fundamental principle. And it is known (Kiddushin 40a) that the sin of idolatry blemishes even in thought, unlike all other transgressions, as it is said (Ezekiel 14:5), "in order to take hold of the house of Israel by their heart" - but concerning other transgressions it is said (Psalms 66:18), "if I regard iniquity in my heart, the LORD will not hear me" - and thought is what blemishes the soul and the throne, and it follows that he uproots himself from holiness and falls from the height of the firmament to the depth of the abyss, which is a strange god. And just as the blemish is through contemplation, so the repair is through the contemplation of repentance - for thoughts of repentance come from the side of the soul, and therefore our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Kiddushin 49b) that one who betroths a woman on condition that he is righteous, even if he was wicked, she is betrothed - perhaps he contemplated repentance. Behold, it follows that through his momentary contemplation, he ascended up to the Throne of Glory, to be called a completely righteous man - for the throne is the place from which the souls of the righteous are hewn.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:35: And these two explanations have a revelation in the Midrash (Pesikta Rabbati, parashah 44); it says: our great teacher expounded, how great is the power of repentance - for as soon as a person contemplates in his heart to repent, at once it ascends and stands before the Throne of Glory - "return, O Israel, to the LORD your God" - the Holy One, blessed be He, said, even if you have sins up to the LORD, up to the Throne of Glory, "return, O Israel" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:36: And it is possible to say another way to resolve this: that excellent repentance is deed, speech, and thought, which correspond to nefesh, ru'ach, and neshamah, as we explained in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 4. And the reason is that when there is a blemish in the nefesh, the ru'ach departs, because it has no throne in which to rest; and since the ru'ach departs, the neshamah also departs to the throne - it follows that the power of repentance must always ascend up to the throne to repair the deed [i.e., the Asiyah level]. And so too, if he did not blemish in deed but blemished in speech, behold, the ru'ach is blemished and the neshamah departs - if so, in returning he must repair the ru'ach and intend to draw down the neshamah. And so if he blemished in thought, in the aspects we explained in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 5, which is a blemish in the neshamah itself, in the very essence of the throne - he must ascend up to the throne itself to repair what he blemished.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:37: Further, concerning the aspects of repentance, he explained in Parashat Naso (Zohar, page 123a), of blessed memory: now we must return to the gate of repentance - for is repentance of one kind, that all people who do it become entirely good? But not all faces are alike. There is a person who is completely wicked all his days, and transgresses several negative commandments, and regrets and confesses them, and afterward does neither good nor evil - to this one certainly the Holy One, blessed be He, will forgive, but not that he merit the supernal repentance. There is a person who, after returning from his sins and being atoned for, walks the path of the commandments and occupies himself with all his strength in fear and love of the Holy One, blessed be He - this one merits the lower repentance, called "heh," and this is the lower repentance. And there is a person who, after regretting his sins and performing repentance, occupies himself with Torah in fear and love of the Holy One, blessed be He, not in order to receive a reward - this one merits the letter vav, which is the son of yud-heh, and by his name is called "Binah" - and this causes the vav to return to the heh. And the word "teshuvah" is thus: "tashuv vav le-heh" [the vav returns to the heh] - and never does the heh rest in a person, nor the yud, without fear and love, which are yud-heh - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:38: And when you examine the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, closely, you will find in his words the nature of repentance explained, in what appears to be a redundancy in his wording, saying "there is a person who, after returning from his sins, is atoned for" - what is the meaning of "and is atoned for"? Has he not already said "returns from his sins," which certainly implies "he will be atoned for"? Rather, this matter depends on the four categories of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael would expound (Yoma 86a): that if he transgressed a negative commandment, he is not atoned for until the Day of Atonement - for so he said, if a person transgressed a negative commandment, repentance suspends and the Day of Atonement atones; and if he transgressed [something warranting] karet or death by the court, repentance and the Day of Atonement suspend and suffering finishes the atonement. It follows that he is not atoned for except through suffering. And so they also said further on, "there is a person who regrets his sins and performs repentance" - this is redundant, but it is along the lines explained, that one must perform repentance for each and every transgression, and afflict himself with fasting and self-mortification, as we shall copy below the repentances of Rabbi Elazar of Germaiza, peace be upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:39: And from this discourse you further learn two things. The first, that the essential repentance is occupation with Torah in fear and love, through which one merits the supernal repentance - and concerning this we say in our prayer, "return us, our Father, to Your Torah" - for one distant from Torah is distant from the Holy One, blessed be He, and "an ignorant person cannot be pious, nor a boor fear sin" - and therefore the essence of repentance is in occupying oneself with Torah, for the Torah teaches him how to return to appease his Owner, and not stumble again. And the second, that before he occupies himself with Torah, he must first have regret and repentance - and this is what it says, "after regretting his sins and performing repentance, he occupies himself with Torah" - behold, before regret and repentance, his Torah is not desired and accepted, as he says (Psalms 50:16), "but to the wicked God says, what right have you to declare My statutes?" And likewise, "anyone who has a blemish shall not approach" (Leviticus 21:18) - and if this one reeks with the filth of his iniquities, how shall he approach before the King? On the contrary, the King will distance Himself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:40: And to this the pious Rabbi Yehuda bar Ila'i, peace be upon him, referred in saying (cf. Berachot 17a), happy is he whose labor is in Torah and who gives satisfaction to his Creator - meaning, that one who is occupied with it is clean of sin and iniquity, for then the King delights in him and in his Torah. And this was the virtue of the ancients, whose Torah was so acceptable that they were even exempt from prayer (Shabbat 11a), because their Torah was clean. But one who is full of the stench of the filth of his iniquities - his Torah gives no satisfaction to his Creator. And the reason is that through occupation with Torah, a person draws the Shechinah upon him, and when he is clean of sin, the Shechinah finds a throne and a seat in which to sit and rest, like a person sitting in a properly prepared chair, which gives him satisfaction - so the Torah needs a clean, prepared throne to draw the Shechinah to rest upon it; but when a person is soiled with the stains of his iniquities, the Torah does not rest in him, for there is no throne in him for either the Torah or the Shechinah to rest, since every sin is a painful thorn and a hurtful barb to the one sitting on the throne. Therefore he must first wash away the filth of his iniquities through repentance properly, and afterward occupy himself with Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:41: And he should take an example from this ruling in the Gemara (Berachot 25a) and in the halachic authorities (Rambam, Laws of the Shema, chapter 3, halachah 12; Tur Orach Chaim, section 79): that in a place with a bad odor, it is forbidden to occupy oneself there with Torah and prayer, and one must distance himself four cubits from where the odor ends. So it is with one occupied in Torah while the impurity of the filth of his iniquities is upon him - for all the supernal holy ones distance themselves. And it is known that iniquities are called filth, as it is written (Isaiah 4:4), "when the LORD shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion." And so you find that the Torah did not avail Doeg or Achitophel, for neither of them has a share in the World to Come, even though they expounded several halachot with a "flying tower" [prodigious analytical skill], as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in Chagigah (15b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:42: And the essence of Torah is repentance and deed, and the punishment of a Torah scholar who sins is greater than that of an ignorant person - as we learn in the chapter "Eilu Metziot" (Bava Metzia, end of chapter 2): Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Ila'i expounded, "and declare to My people their transgression" (Isaiah 58:1), and so on - these are the Torah scholars, for whom even unwitting errors are made like willful sins; "and to the house of Jacob, their sins" - these are the ignorant, for whom willful sins are made like unwitting errors - and this is what we learn: Rabbi Yehuda says, be careful with study, for an error in study amounts to a willful sin - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:43: And having explained the nature of repentance, let us explain its boundaries, so that repentance be complete:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:1: It is fitting to know that although we have said that the Holy One, blessed be He, accepts the repentance of those who return, the intent is not the abandonment of the sin alone, and regret alone - rather, one must weigh in his mind the nature of the transgression he committed: whether it is among those liable for negative commandments, or among those liable for karet and death by the court, or the profanation of the Name - these being the four categories of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael would expound (Yoma 86a), whose words we have already copied in the Gate of Love, chapter 12, and in the Gate of Fear, the last chapter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:2: And although Rabbi Yishmael said, "if a person transgressed a positive commandment and repented, he does not move from there until he is forgiven" - one must examine the weight of the commandment, which commandment was nullified. For we find that Reuben disturbed his father's bed, blemishing his father's honor, and prevented him, according to the view of the Kabbalists, from procreation - and there is support for this in the Zohar, Parashat Vayishlach (page 176a) - see there. And we find that he afflicted himself with sackcloth and fasting, as they said in Bereshit Rabbah (84:19), in these words: "and Reuben returned to the pit" (Genesis 37:29) - and where had he been? Rabbi Eliezer says, occupied with his sackcloth and his fast; once he had finished, he went to the pit. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: never before has a person sinned before Me and repented - and you opened the way of repentance; by your life, a descendant of your descendants shall stand and open with repentance - and who is this? Hosea, as it is said (Hosea 14:2), "return, O Israel, to the LORD your God" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:3: And should you say, but we wrote above (chapter 1) that Adam, the first man, and Cain opened with repentance - one may say that they opened with repentance for a negative commandment, and Reuben for a positive commandment, as we have explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:4: Further, they said in the Sifrei (Parashat Va'etchanan), on the verse "Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God," and so on - they said there, concerning what Jacob our father, peace be upon him, said (Genesis 28:21), "then the LORD shall be my God" - that His Name should rest upon me, that no unfitness go forth from me from beginning to end. And so it says (ibid. 35:22), "and it came to pass, while Israel dwelt in that land" - once Jacob heard [of Reuben's act], he trembled, saying, perhaps some unfitness has occurred among my sons - until he was informed by the Holy One, blessed be He, that Reuben had repented, as it is said, "now the sons of Jacob were twelve" - and did we not already know that they were twelve? Rather, he was informed that he had repented - to teach you that Reuben fasted all his days, until Moses came and accepted him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:6), "let Reuben live, and not die" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:5: Further, concerning the matter of King David's repentance, peace be upon him, Scripture testifies (1 Kings 15:5) that "nothing was found against him except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite" - meaning that Uriah was killed by the sword of the children of Ammon, as they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Mishpatim, page 107a), for the matter of Bathsheba was entirely permitted, since every man who went out to David's wars would write a bill of divorce for his wife, as they further elaborated in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit, pages 8a-b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:6: And our Rabbis said (Avodah Zarah 4b), in these words: David was not fit for that deed, as it is said (Psalms 109:22), "and my heart is wounded within me" - rather, so that if an individual sins, they say to him, behold, David sinned and the Holy One, blessed be He, accepted him. And so he himself said (ibid. 51:15), "then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners shall return to You" - as explained there in Parashat Mishpatim on the aforementioned page. And so they said in Midrash Tanchuma (Midrash Tehillim, Psalm 40), "many shall see and fear" (Psalms 40:4) - whoever wishes to repent, let him look at David; and so it says (Isaiah 55:4), "behold, I have given him for a witness to the peoples" - immediately, "and shall trust in the LORD" (Psalms ibid.) - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:7: And behold, the matter of King David's repentance, peace be upon him, is explained in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, and also in the Book of Psalms. Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Sanhedrin, chapter Chelek (107a): for six months David suffered from leprosy, as it is said (Psalms 51:14), "restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and let a willing spirit uphold me." And from where do we derive these six months? For it is written (1 Kings 2:11), "and the days that David reigned over Israel were forty years; seven years he reigned in Hebron, and thirty-three years he reigned in Jerusalem" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:8: Further, in Tanna D'Vei Eliyahu (Rabbah, chapter 2), concerning his repentance, on the verse (2 Samuel 23:1), "now these are the last words of David" - in these words: another interpretation, "these are the last words of David" - he said before Him, Master of the universe, just as You forgave my former iniquities, so forgive me my later iniquities. Another interpretation: for twenty-two years the holy spirit departed from David, king of Israel, and every single day he would shed a cup of tears and eat his bread with ashes, as it is said (Psalms 102:10), "for I have eaten ashes like bread." Another interpretation: he said before Him, Master of the universe, accept me in repentance, so that You may rebuke the wicked and say to them: if David, king of Israel, who did before Me so grave a thing, once he returned in repentance before Me, I accepted him - how much more so I would accept you! And so he says (Psalms 51:6), "against You, You only, have I sinned," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:9: Further, in Tanna D'Vei Eliyahu, found among us in manuscript, in these words: "now King David was old, advanced in years, and they covered him with clothes" (1 Kings 1:1) - this is what Scripture says (Isaiah 40:31), "but those who wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength." Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: for thirteen years David lay ill, confined to his bed, and seven cushions would be changed beneath him every day because of the abundant discharge that flowed from his body - this is what is written (Psalms 6:7), "I make my bed swim" - these thirteen years of suffering were because of the deed he did with Bathsheba, and all his enemies would say, when will he die? This is what Scripture says (ibid. 41:6), "my enemies speak evil of me: when shall he die, and his name perish?" And when he heard this, he gave his soul over to prayer and supplication, and sought mercy before the Holy One, blessed be He, and said: Master of the universe, sustain me for the sake of the Temple that Samuel the prophet entrusted to me, and please strengthen me and give me courage and raise me up, and bring me down from this bed in peace, and I will complete for them my scroll - the building of the Temple. Immediately the Holy One, blessed be He, heard his prayer, and he arose from his bed, as it is said (1 Chronicles 28:2), "and David the king stood up upon his feet" - and where else does a person stand if not on his feet? What is "upon his feet"? This teaches that he was healed and stood healthy - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:10: Further, a penitent must impose upon himself a rebuke for at least one hour a day, as we find King David, peace be upon him, did - and so they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Mishpatim, page 107b), in these words: and it is written (2 Samuel 15:30), "and David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and wept as he went up, and had his head covered, and he went barefoot." Head covered, and barefoot - why? Rather, he was rebuked, and he made himself rebuked to accept his punishment, and the people distanced themselves four cubits from him. Happy is the servant who serves his Master this way, who recognizes his sin, to return from it in complete repentance. Come and see, even more so was what Shim'i ben Gera did to him, of all the distresses that passed over him until that day, and David did not respond to him with a word, for this was fitting for him, and through this his iniquities were atoned for. Now one must consider - Shim'i was a Torah scholar with great wisdom - why did he go out toward David and do to him all that he did? Rather, the matter came from another place, and it was put into his heart, and all this for David's benefit - for that which Shim'i did to him caused him to enter into complete repentance, and broke him with great breaking, and he shed abundant tears from within his heart before the Holy One, blessed be He - and concerning this it is said (2 Samuel 16:10), "for the LORD has said to him, curse" - he knew that the matter descended from a supernal place - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:11: And from the general discourse another lesson emerges for the penitent, that he should hear his disgrace and not respond, along the lines of David. And the reason is that the one who disgraces him is a messenger sent from above to disgrace him, and he must accept the judgment with a pleasant countenance - for behold, David did not have those very insults that Shim'i ben Gera said to him, and nevertheless he was silent and accepted it - all the more so one who has sinned and greatly transgressed, for whom it is possible that everything said of him is true, in proportion to the supernal blemish he has caused.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:12: And so they further explained, further on (Parashat Mishpatim, page 108, on this verse), that the repair of the Shechinah is a broken and contrite heart, and through sadness and bitterness one sacrifices [subdues] the judgment - for the evil inclination grows strong in a person's heart from the side of judgment, where its root is, and since the heart is humbled, this indicates that judgment is subdued and bound beneath Chesed. Further, when a person sinned and brought a sacrifice, it was through the attribute of mercy that his sacrifice was accepted, for judgment dictates that the sinning soul shall die - but through the attribute of mercy the Holy One, blessed be He, said, let him bring an animal's soul in place of his own soul. And concerning this, it is not written of the sacrifices, "a sacrifice to Elohim," but "to YHVH," who is mercy - and what is the sacrifice offered to Elohim? "A broken spirit" - for he actually sacrifices himself and his inclination in the breaking of his heart and bitterness and sadness, as though dead - for that heart that grew strong in sin is already broken and dead - it follows that he actually offers up his soul that dwells in the heart, and this is the sacrifice that Elohim desires. And through this his words there are understood, in these words: "for You do not desire sacrifice, else would I give it" - does the Holy One, blessed be He, not desire that sacrifices be brought before Him? He has indeed established for the wicked a sacrifice, that they bring it and their iniquities be atoned for - but David said "before Elohim," and sacrifice is not brought to the name "Elohim" but to the name YHVH - for concerning the harsh attribute of judgment, sacrifices are not brought, as it is written (Leviticus 1:2), "when any man of you brings an offering to the LORD" - "to the LORD," and not to the name "Elohim"; "and when you bring a meal-offering to the LORD" - "a thanksgiving sacrifice to the LORD, a peace-offering to the LORD" - and therefore, since King David spoke "before Elohim," it was necessary to write (Psalms 51:18), "for You do not desire sacrifice, else would I give it; You do not delight in burnt offering" - for to this name only "a broken spirit" is brought near, as it is written, "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" - the sacrifice of Elohim is sadness and a broken heart; and therefore, whoever dreams a bad dream needs sadness and a broken spirit, and that sadness suffices for the bad dream, and judgment does not rule over him, for he has offered before it a sacrifice fitting for the attribute of judgment. "And a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise" - what is "You will not despise"? It follows that there is a heart that is despised - is that not the heart that is proud, a heart with haughtiness of spirit? This is a heart that is despised - but "a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:13: And among the things the penitent must repair is the sign of the covenant, blemished through the emission of seed in vain - from which no one in our time is saved in his youth. And they said in the Zohar that David was punished because he did not guard the sign of the covenant as is fitting - in these words, in the Zohar (Parashat Lech Lecha, end of page 43): another verse opened and said, "though a host encamp against me," and so on (Psalms 27:3) - we have thus learned, "in this I trust" - what is "in this" [be-zot]? This is the sign of the covenant that is always present with a person and alluded to above, and therefore it is said "be-zot," as it is written (Genesis 9:12), "this [zot] is the sign of the covenant," "this [zot] is My covenant" (ibid. 17:10) - and it is all one level. And we have learned, "zeh" and "zot" are on one level and are not separated. And should you say, if so, are not the rest of the people of the world the same? Why David alone, and not another? Rather, because it is grasped and alluded to in him, and it is the crown of Malchut. Come and see, because David the king did not guard this "zot" as is fitting, the kingship was removed from him for that entire time; and thus we have learned, this "zot" is alluded to in the supernal Malchut, and alluded to in Jerusalem, the holy city. At that hour David transgressed concerning it, a voice went forth and said, in that which you were bound, you shall be released - you will be driven from Jerusalem, and the kingship shall be removed from you - and so it was: in that which a person transgresses, he is punished. And if it was so for King David, how much more so for the rest of the people of the world! - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:14: Behold, it is explicit that David received punishment because of the blemish of the covenant, and all his Torah and deeds did not stand for him to save him, and he was punished measure for measure, as explained in the discourse. And so every person is fitting to accept upon himself suffering to purify what he has blemished, and it is fitting that he exile himself, measure for measure, along the lines of David - and as they said, exile atones for everything (Sanhedrin 37b) - see there. And from this the reader may infer concerning the other iniquities, that all of them require cleansing through suffering.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:15: And in the Zohar (Parashat Vayikra, end of page 23) they further explained this matter concerning David's being punished, in these words: and should you say, David, who would rise at midnight - why was judgment aroused against him? Rather, David was different, for he transgressed against that to which he was bound, and required judgment, and by that which he transgressed he was judged - he sinned against the holy kingship and against holy Jerusalem, and was driven from Jerusalem, and the kingship was removed from him, until he repaired himself properly and was punished. Rabbi Yehuda said, why did the Holy One, blessed be He, punish David through his own son, as it is written (2 Samuel 12:11), "behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house"? Rabbi Yosi said, we have already established this - because if another person were to rise against him, he would not have mercy on him. He said to him, but did not Absalom seek to kill his father with several plots he devised against him? He said to him, I have not heard [that reason]; I have heard [another]: David sinned with Bathsheba without qualification - the Holy One, blessed be He, said, let a son come from the daughter of a foreign god and take his vengeance - and who is this? Absalom, who descended from "a beautiful captive woman" (Deuteronomy 21:11) that was taken in. From here we learn: whoever takes such a woman in war and desires her, in the end a "stubborn and rebellious son" comes forth from her - why? Because the impurity has not yet departed from her - and this has already been established - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:16: And what he said, "David sinned with Bathsheba without qualification" [stam], means with the lower Bathsheba and the supernal Bathsheba - and the blemish of Bathsheba was that she ate unripe fruit, meaning that he enjoyed the world without a blessing, as they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Tazria, end of page 45), and we shall copy his words below - and this is what Scripture attests (2 Samuel 12:12), "for you did it secretly," and so on.
